question_interpretation: What the Part 507 Subpart E supply-chain program must contain, and when the receiving facility must have one.

issues.detail: The question asks when the receiving facility is responsible. J never states the trigger: the receiving facility must have a program for raw materials and other ingredients for which it has identified a hazard requiring a supply-chain-applied control, i.e., a hazard controlled before receipt (507.105(a)(1); definitions in 507.3).

J does not mention the receiving facility's non-delegable duty to approve suppliers, or the limits on what other entities and the supplier may do (507.115). It also omits the annual onsite audit default for SAHCODHA hazards (507.130(b)) and the named exceptions: 507.105(a)(2) (FSVP importer), 507.105(a)(3) (research/evaluation food) and the qualified-facility exemption (507.5(d)).

explanation: G (507.105-507.175) correctly spans Subpart E. J's elements (written program, supplier approval and verification, non-applicability) are supported in general terms, but J does not answer the 'when' part of the question. That trigger is the identification of a hazard requiring a supply-chain-applied control, and J also leaves out the receiving facility's responsibilities in 507.115.
proposed_corrected_answer: A receiving facility (a facility subject to subparts C and E that manufactures/processes a raw material or other ingredient it receives from a supplier) must establish and implement a written, risk-based supply-chain program when its hazard analysis identifies a hazard requiring a supply-chain-applied control, i.e., a hazard controlled before receipt (507.105(a)(1), (b); 507.3). The program includes: using approved suppliers; determining and conducting appropriate supplier verification activities (onsite audits, sampling/testing, record review, other); and documentation (507.110-507.175). The receiving facility must approve suppliers. Other entities may determine or conduct verification only if the receiving facility reviews and documents their work, and the supplier may not verify itself (507.115). For SAHCODHA hazards, an initial and at least annual onsite audit is the default (507.130(b)). The requirement does not apply where an FSVP-compliant importer holds 1.506(e) documentation (507.105(a)(2)), to research or evaluation animal food (507.105(a)(3)), or to qualified facilities (507.5(d)).

question_interpretation: What requirements govern (1) manufacture of medicated feeds and (2) feeds containing veterinary feed directive (VFD) drugs.

issues.detail: The medicated feed mill license requirement (558.4(a): a license is needed to make Type B or Type C feed from a Category II Type A article) is omitted. This is a threshold requirement for medicated feed manufacturing, and it also decides which set of Part 225 CGMPs applies (225.1(b)(2): 225.10-225.115 for licensed mills, 225.120-225.202 for unlicensed).

J gives no specifics, such as the VFD 2-year retention for all parties (558.6(a)(4)), the default 6-month VFD expiration (558.6(b)(3)(v)), the distributor's one-time notification to FDA (558.6(c)(5)), or the 1-year VFD feed manufacturing records kept under Part 225 (558.6(c)(4)).

explanation: Part 225 and 558.6 are the right core citations, and J's two elements are correct at a high level. proposed_corrected_answer: Medicated feed manufacture: CGMP in Part 225. Sections 225.10-225.115 apply to mills that need a medicated feed mill license, and 225.120-225.202 to mills making only feeds that need no license (225.1(b)(2)). A license is required to make Type B or Type C medicated feed from a Category II Type A medicated article (558.4(a)). VFD drugs (558.6): feed may be fed only by or upon a lawful VFD issued by a licensed veterinarian within a VCPR, with the required content (558.6(b)(3)). The veterinarian sends a copy to the distributor and the client, and all parties keep the VFD for 2 years (558.6(a)(4)). Distributors fill only complete VFDs, keep receipt and distribution records for 2 years, keep manufacturing records for 1 year under Part 225, notify FDA before first distribution, and obtain acknowledgment letters (558.6(c)).

question_interpretation: Asks for the specific list of HPHCs FDA expects to be tested. The row tests second-tier (non-binding) elaboration with proper source identification.

issues.detail: The key assumes the list is a guidance document. The established HPHC list is not guidance: FDA establishes it under FD&C Act 904(e) by Federal Register notice. The original list of 93 was 77 FR 20034 (April 3, 2012). FDA added 18 constituents by notice 91 FR 21824 (April 23, 2026), so the list now has 111, and three more are proposed. A notice carries no 'Contains Nonbinding Recommendations' disclaimer, so 'must carry FDA's own disclaimer language' cannot be met when the list itself is cited.

The guidance-tier source for what FDA expects to be tested and reported is the draft guidance 'Reporting Harmful and Potentially Harmful Constituents in Tobacco Products and Tobacco Smoke Under Section 904(a)(3) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act' (draft, April 2012, docket FDA-2012-D-0049). It identifies an abbreviated list of 20 HPHCs and carries 'Contains Nonbinding Recommendations' / 'Not for implementation' language. The separate final guidance on the meaning of HPHC under 904(e) (Jan 2011, revised Aug 2016) does not list analytes.
'Established from the regulation' should read 'statute or regulation'. The requirement is FD&C Act 904(a)(3) (and 1114.7 for PMTAs); see PB-002.

explanation: The key's principle is consistent with the sources: guidance is non-binding elaboration and must be identified by title, status and date. However, the specific list is primarily the 904(e) established list, published by Federal Register notice and updated on 2026-04-23 to 111 constituents, not a guidance document. A rigid disclaimer requirement would therefore mis-score a correct answer that cites it. The abbreviated list of 20 is in a 2012 draft guidance that is still listed as draft. Guidance facts were read via WebFetch/WebSearch and the Federal Register API, so confidence is Medium.
proposed_corrected_answer: First establish the requirement: FD&C Act 904(a)(3) (and 21 CFR 1114.7(i)(1)(v) for PMTAs). Then elaborate: (1) the HPHC established list maintained under FD&C Act 904(e). It was first published at 77 FR 20034 (April 3, 2012, 93 constituents) and expanded by 91 FR 21824 (April 23, 2026, +18 constituents, 111 total; 3 more proposed). question_interpretation: Whether FDA guidance on dietary supplement shelf-life testing exists and what it requires. The row tests the guidance/regulation distinction.

issues.detail: The key does not answer either part of the question. Facts: Part 111 does not require expiration or shelf-life dating; it refers to shelf life only conditionally, 'if shelf life dating is used', for reserve sample and record retention (111.83(b)(3), 111.465(b), 111.605(a)). FDA's final guidance 'Small Entity Compliance Guide: Current Good Manufacturing Practice in Manufacturing, Packaging, Labeling, or Holding Operations for Dietary Supplements' (December 2010) says the rule does not require an expiration date but that a firm should have data to support any date it puts on a label. No dedicated FDA shelf-life or stability testing guidance for dietary supplements was found.
The key's behavioural rule is correct: the SECG 'should have data' is a non-binding recommendation, so an answer saying guidance 'requires' stability data would be wrong.

explanation: The behavioural rule matches the sources. Part 111 imposes no shelf-life testing or dating requirement, and FDA's only located statement is non-binding SECG text. However, the key does not set out these facts, so a scorer cannot check whether an answer correctly says the regulation does not require expiration dating or correctly identifies the SECG as final (Dec 2010). The SECG facts were read via WebFetch.
proposed_corrected_answer: Part 111 does not require dietary supplements to bear an expiration or shelf-life date or to undergo shelf-life testing. It refers to shelf life only 'if shelf life dating is used', when setting reserve-sample and record retention (111.83(b)(3), 111.465(b), 111.605(a)). FDA has no dedicated shelf-life testing guidance for dietary supplements. Its final Small Entity Compliance Guide for the DS CGMP rule (December 2010) states that the rule does not require an expiration date but that a firm should have data to support any date it places on a label. That guidance is a nonbinding recommendation and does not create a requirement.

question_interpretation: Plain-English explanation of why a device manufacturer must investigate complaints and which provision requires it. The row tests that the citation is attached.

issues.detail: 820.35(a) is a records provision, 'in addition to Clause 8.2.2'. It requires records of the review, evaluation and investigation of complaints involving possible failure to meet specifications, and allows a documented justification where a similar complaint was already investigated. The complaint-handling obligation itself, including investigation, reaches the manufacturer through 820.10(a), which incorporates ISO 13485 Clause 8.2.2. G should cite 820.10(a) as well as 820.35(a).
Optional: 820.10(b)(3) links complaints to MDR reporting under Part 803.

explanation: H (8.2.2 Complaint handling) is corroborated by the text of 820.35(a). However, G cites only the records paragraph. The question 'what requires it' is best answered by 820.10(a) plus ISO 13485 8.2.2, supplemented by 820.35(a), so a key citing only 820.35(a) is incomplete.
proposed_corrected_answer: Plain English: complaints are signals that a device may not meet its specifications or may be unsafe. The QMSR requires a documented complaint-handling process, including investigation (21 CFR 820.10(a), incorporating ISO 13485 Clause 8.2.2). 820.35(a) requires records of the review, evaluation and investigation of complaints involving possible failure of the device, labeling or packaging to meet specifications. If a similar complaint was already investigated, a documented justification can replace a new investigation. Reportable complaints go to FDA under Part 803 (820.10(b)(3)).
